newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher despite strong NAPM data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher despite strong NAPM data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended mainly higher on Monday, recovering from losses incurred after stronger-than-expected U.S. manufacturing-sector data.

The market opened on a strong note as buyers followed through on strength seen late last week. Also constructive, economists said, was the dollar's rise against the German mark after a Socialist electoral victory in France raised doubts about potential strength of the planned Euro currency.
Government data on U.S. personal income and spending in April were weak. Income and spending each rose 0.1 percent.
At mid-morning, however, a strong May National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) report intercepted the market's upward momentum, quashing it and sending the market into reverse.

Economists said the May NAPM index, which rose to 57.1 from 54.2 in April, topped their forecasts. Opinion has been divided over whether slower economic activity in April was the start of a slowing trend or just a pause after the first quarter's fast economic growth pace. Just before the NAPM report, the government reported a 1.0 percent decline in construction spending in April, the first drop in four months.
"The personal income and spending data and the construction drop reflected April activity and the market had discounted a soft April," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
The more current May NAPM report seemed to support the view that the weaker economy in April had been temporary.

"NAPM caught the market really, really off guard," said Elliott Platt, managing director in charge of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "It was dominated by a sharp upward move in new orders. Supplier delivery times lengthened and inventories jumped."

David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co., said the NAPM report hinted that the economy would "rebound and see accelerating growth and a greater potential for inflation pressures in the second half of the year."
Given that rosy economic scenario, the inflation-wary bond market performed surprisingly well on Monday, analysts said.

"There was some hedge fund selling of five-year maturities and some bank selling in the short end," said Stiles. "But some buying in the futures market took us back up to the 200-day moving average of 109-23 in September T-bonds."

Economists said the possibility that seasonal factors could depress the May U.S. payroll employment figure due this Friday might also have helped the market to recover from the setback dealt it by the robust NAPM report.
"It looks like the May employment report could help the market," said Platt, who estimated payrolls expanded by a modest 150,000 jobs in May as the unemployment rate ticked up to 5.1 percent.
"The only wild card in the (employment report) deck is hourly earnings," said Platt. "When hourly earnings have been down, as they were in April, there's the risk of a snapback."
At the close, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was at 96-10/32, up 2/32 from Friday's close to yield 6.90 percent.
Ten-year notes ended at 99-24/32, up 1/32 to yield 6.66 percent. Five-year notes closed unchanged at 99-31/32, yielding 6.51 percent.
At the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes ended unchanged at 100-2/32, yielding 6.22 percent.
Three-month bill rates closed at 4.74 percent, down 11 basis points. Six-month bill rates finished at 5.18 percent, down one basis point. Year bill rates ended unchanged at 5.46 percent.
